title: Equations with fractions & brackets
examples: What is the first step when I see fractions in an equation?
How do I check if my answer for x is correct?
Do I multiply everything by the largest denominator?

explain.say: Today we will solve equations that have fractions and brackets. First we learn to clear the denominators. This means getting rid of the fractions entirely.
To clear the denominators we find the least common multiple of all the denominators. Then we multiply every single term by this number.
Let us look at an example equation. It is x over 2 plus x over 3 equals 7. The denominators are two and three.
The least common multiple of two and three is six. So we multiply every term by six. This gives us threex plus twox equals forty two.
Now we solve the simple equation. Combining the x terms gives us fivex equals forty two. Dividing by five gives x equals eighty four divided by five.

faq.q: Do I have to multiply every single term by the LCM?
faq.a: Yes you must multiply every single term by the least common multiple. This keeps the equation balanced and removes all fractions.
asks: Do I multiply by the denominators?

faq.q: What if there are brackets in the equation?
faq.a: First you must expand the brackets using the distributive law. Then you can find the least common multiple to clear the fractions.

faq.q: How do I check if my solution for x is correct?
faq.a: You substitute the value you found for x back into the original equation. If both sides are equal, your solution is correct.
asks: How do I check my answer?

faq.q: Can I just multiply the denominators together?
faq.a: No you should find the least common multiple. Multiplying them together might give you a much larger number than necessary.
asks: What is the best number to multiply by?

faq.q: What if one denominator is already one?
faq.a: If a denominator is one, you can just ignore it when finding the least common multiple. It does not affect the process.
asks: Does a denominator of one matter?
Can I skip denominators of one?

facts: To clear denominators, find the least common multiple of all denominators.
Multiply every term in the equation by this least common multiple.
Remember to expand any brackets before clearing the denominators.
To check a solution, substitute the value back into the original equation.

quiz.say: If you have x / 3 + x / 6 = 5, what is the LCM?
quiz.why: The denominators are three and six. The smallest number that both three and six divide into is six.

wrong.1: This is wrong because six is a multiple of three, so three is too small.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you multiplied the denominators together.
wrong.3: This is wrong because you divided the denominators instead of finding the LCM.

quiz.say: If x = 7 is the solution, what must the original equation look like?
quiz.why: If x equals seven, then x plus one equals eight. This is the simplest form of checking.

wrong.0: This is wrong because you subtracted one from the seven.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you are just stating the value, not checking the equation.
wrong.3: This is wrong because you forgot to add one to the seven.
